title: Preprocessing and feature selection belong inside the cross-validation loop

effect.statement: When a step fits a model with cross-validation: scaling, imputation, and feature selection must happen inside the loop, never before the split. A selection over all samples first biases the performance estimate upward by some AUC points, and nothing errors.

recommendation: Use a pipeline construction that refits the preprocessing inside each fold, and report the nested-CV estimate.

sources.citation: Ambroise C, McLachlan GJ (2002) Selection bias in gene extraction on the basis of microarray gene-expression data. PNAS 99:6562-6566
Varma S, Simon R (2006) Bias in error estimation when using cross-validation for model selection. BMC Bioinformatics 7:91

title: A feature list from an upstream step on the same samples is already a selection

effect.statement: When a step builds a panel from features that an upstream step selected on the same samples: that list is already a selection over all samples, and a panel built from it leaks. Build the panel from the full feature matrix, and select again inside cross-validation. If only the pre-selected list is available, report the performance estimate as optimistic, and say why.

sources.citation: Ambroise C, McLachlan GJ (2002) Selection bias in gene extraction. PNAS 99:6562-6566
Kaufman S, Rosset S, Perlich C, Stitelman O (2012) Leakage in data mining: formulation, detection, and avoidance. ACM TKDD 6:15

title: Report the multiplicity-corrected p-value for an optimized cutpoint

effect.statement: When a step dichotomizes a continuous biomarker at an optimized cutpoint: the maximum of a log-rank statistic over many candidate cutpoints is not chi-squared distributed, thus the nominal p-value of the best split is meaningless. Report the multiplicity-corrected p-value from maximally selected rank statistics, the cutpoint, and the group sizes on either side. Do not optimize the cutpoint on the same data that the performance is reported on.

sources.citation: Altman DG, Lausen B, Sauerbrei W, Schumacher M (1994) Dangers of using optimal cutpoints in the evaluation of prognostic factors. JNCI 86:829-835
Hothorn T, Lausen B (2003) On the exact distribution of maximally selected rank statistics. Computational Statistics and Data Analysis 43:121-137

title: Do a check of the proportional-hazards assumption, and repair a failure

effect.statement: When a step fits a Cox model: the proportional-hazards assumption is necessary. Do a check of it with the scaled Schoenfeld residuals. If the check fails for a covariate, stratify on it or add a time-varying term, and report the hazard ratio as time-averaged, not as a constant effect.

sources.citation: Grambsch PM, Therneau TM (1994) Proportional hazards tests and diagnostics based on weighted residuals. Biometrika 81:515-526

title: Call a biomarker predictive only on a significant treatment-marker interaction

effect.statement: When a step calls a biomarker predictive: a prognostic marker associates with the outcome regardless of treatment, and a predictive marker needs a significant treatment-by-marker interaction term. Do not call a marker predictive without that test, and a single-arm study cannot produce the interaction at all.

sources.citation: Ballman KV (2015) Biomarker: predictive or prognostic? Journal of Clinical Oncology 33:3968-3971

title: Prefer a simple model below 100 samples

effect.statement: When a step fits a prediction model below about 100 samples: prefer a simple model, which is logistic regression, or Cox for survival. A tree ensemble overfits on a small N, and a prediction model needs many events for each candidate parameter.

sources.citation: Riley RD et al. (2020) Calculating the sample size required for developing a clinical prediction model. BMJ 368:m441
van der Ploeg T, Austin PC, Steyerberg EW (2014) Modern modelling techniques are data hungry. BMC Medical Research Methodology 14:137
